name: Hiroshima and Miyajima
tagline: A city that rebuilt itself around a direct, deliberate reckoning with its history, beside an island shrine considered one of Japan's three most scenic views.
highlight: Itsukushima Shrine's vermillion torii gate, appearing to float on the water at high tide off Miyajima's shore.
shortDescription: Hiroshima's honest confrontation with the atomic bombing, paired with Miyajima island's floating torii gate, one of Japan's most iconic views.
metaDescription: A Hiroshima and Miyajima travel guide: the Peace Memorial Park, the Atomic Bomb Dome, the floating torii gate, when to go and a practical two-day itinerary.
knownFor: The Atomic Bomb Dome, Itsukushima's floating torii, oysters
goodFor: History, reflection, scenic island day trips

image.alt: Itsukushima Shrine's vermillion torii gate appearing to float at high tide off Miyajima

intro: Hiroshima was destroyed by the world's first wartime use of a nuclear weapon on 6 August 1945, and the city's rebuilding since has been shaped by a genuine, deliberate commitment to remembrance and peace advocacy rather than simply moving past the event. The Peace Memorial Park and its museum present this history directly, and the city has become a genuine global centre for nuclear disarmament advocacy as a result.

That history sits alongside a rebuilt, lively modern city — wide boulevards, a well-regarded food scene built around its own distinct okonomiyaki style, and a population that has, in the decades since, built something resilient and forward-looking rather than defined solely by tragedy.

Miyajima, a short ferry ride away, offers real contrast: officially Itsukushima, the island is considered one of Japan's three most scenic views, its shrine's torii gate appearing to float on the water at high tide, a serene counterpart to Hiroshima's weightier history.

whyVisit.intro: The pairing's case is that no other Japan itinerary combines this direct a reckoning with history alongside this serene a natural and religious site.

points.title: The history is presented with real honesty
points.text: The Peace Memorial Park and Museum address the atomic bombing directly, an essential, moving part of understanding modern Japan.

points.title: Miyajima's torii gate is one of Japan's iconic images
points.text: Considered one of the country's three most scenic views for centuries, and it lives up to the reputation in person.

points.title: The city itself is resilient and lively
points.text: Rebuilt into a modern, forward-looking city with a distinct food culture, not simply a memorial site.

points.title: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is worth the trip alone
points.text: A layered, noodle-added variation distinct from Osaka's version, with real local pride attached to it.

points.title: The pairing is easy
points.text: Miyajima sits under an hour from central Hiroshima by tram and ferry, making the combination simple to fit into a wider itinerary.

attractionsIntro: Hiroshima's memorial sites and Miyajima's shrine and mountain, together forming one of Japan's most meaningful pairings.

attractions.name: Peace Memorial Park
attractions.text: A moving landscaped park built around the hypocentre area, home to the Children's Peace Monument, the eternal flame and the Cenotaph for the atomic bomb victims.
attractions.tip: The park is worth a slow, unhurried walk rather than a rushed pass-through between the Dome and the museum.

attractions.name: The Atomic Bomb Dome (Genbaku Dome)

image.alt: The preserved ruin of the Atomic Bomb Dome in Hiroshima

attractions.text: The skeletal ruin of a former exhibition hall, deliberately preserved in its bombed state as a permanent, powerful reminder, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
attractions.tip: The view across the river at dusk, with the Dome lit against the darkening sky, is striking and less crowded than daytime.

attractions.name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum

image.alt: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum building

attractions.text: An unflinching museum presenting the bombing's human impact through artefacts and testimony, essential context alongside the park's memorials.
attractions.tip: Allow at least two hours — the museum's content is substantial and deserves unhurried time.

attractions.name: Itsukushima Shrine's floating torii gate

image.file: File:The Torii gate of the Itsukushima shrine- it gets partially submerged during high tide (49494998183).jpg
image.alt: Itsukushima Shrine's torii gate partially submerged at high tide

attractions.text: A vermillion torii gate standing in the water off Miyajima's shore, appearing to float at high tide, one of Japan's most photographed and historically revered images.
attractions.tip: Check tide tables ahead — high tide gives the floating effect, while low tide lets you walk out to the gate itself.

attractions.name: Mount Misen, Miyajima

image.file: File:MY - View from Mount Misen on Miyajima, Japan, 2015.jpg
image.alt: The view across the Seto Inland Sea from Mount Misen

attractions.text: The island's sacred peak, reachable by cable car and a short hike, offering sweeping views across the Seto Inland Sea.
attractions.tip: The cable car doesn't reach the true summit — a final 30-minute walk is required, well worth the extra effort.

attractions.name: Hiroshima Castle

image.alt: The main gate of the reconstructed Hiroshima Castle

attractions.text: A reconstructed keep on the site of the original, destroyed in the 1945 bombing, its moat and grounds offering a peaceful contrast to the Peace Park's weight.
attractions.tip: The castle's top floor observation deck gives a good orientation view over the wider city.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the memorial sites and the shrine, this pairing rewards Miyajima's wildlife, its mountain views and Hiroshima's own food culture.

thingsToDo.title: Take the ferry to Miyajima

image.file: File:Itsukushima Island, Mt Misen, Torii of Itsukushima Shrine and Ferry for Miyajima Route 001.jpg
image.alt: The ferry approaching Miyajima with the torii gate and Mount Misen in view

thingsToDo.text: A short, scenic crossing from Miyajimaguchi, with the torii gate visible from the boat well before landing.
thingsToDo.tip: JR Pass holders can use the JR-operated ferry at no extra cost, one of the pass's useful smaller benefits.

thingsToDo.title: Hike Mount Misen

image.file: File:Miyajima- Part III - Mount Misen - Miyajima512.jpg
image.alt: The hiking trail up Mount Misen on Miyajima

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding half-day hike or cable-car-plus-short-walk combination, rewarding effort with sweeping island and sea views from the summit.
thingsToDo.tip: Start early if hiking the full route — the ascent takes two to three hours and afternoon heat can make it demanding in summer.

thingsToDo.title: Eat Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki
thingsToDo.text: Layered rather than mixed, with a genuine noodle addition setting it distinctly apart from Osaka's version, cooked directly at teppan counters.
thingsToDo.tip: Okonomimura, a multi-floor building packed with dedicated okonomiyaki stalls, is a fun way to compare several versions in one visit.

thingsToDo.title: Spot Miyajima's deer

image.alt: A sika deer roaming freely on Miyajima

thingsToDo.text: Like Nara, Miyajima is home to freely roaming sacred deer, considered messengers of the island's shrine, relaxed around visitors.
thingsToDo.tip: Unlike Nara, feeding the deer is now discouraged on Miyajima — admire rather than offer food.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Children's Peace Monument

image.file: File:Children's Peace Monument - Hiroshima - Japan - Sarah Stierch.jpg
image.alt: The Children's Peace Monument in Hiroshima

thingsToDo.text: A statue inspired by Sadako Sasaki, a bombing survivor who folded paper cranes hoping for recovery, surrounded by millions of cranes sent from around the world.
thingsToDo.tip: Consider folding and leaving a paper crane yourself — origami paper is often available at nearby shops for this purpose.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Miyajima's old town streets

image.alt: Traditional shopfronts along Miyajima's old town street

thingsToDo.text: Omotesando's shopping street offers good souvenir shopping and food stalls, a lively contrast to the shrine's quiet reverence just beyond it.
thingsToDo.tip: Grilled oysters and momiji manju stalls line the street — both are worth stopping for.

foodIntro: Hiroshima and Miyajima's food culture centres on the region's own okonomiyaki style, oysters and Seto Inland Sea seafood.

foods.name: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki

image.alt: A finished Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki on the teppan grill

foods.text: Layered rather than mixed, built up with cabbage, pork, a generous portion of noodles and a fried egg, distinctly different from Osaka's batter-mixed version.
foods.whereToTry: Okonomimura's multi-floor stall building, or any dedicated teppan counter across the city.

foods.name: Hiroshima oysters

image.file: File:Grilled oysters - Food in Miyajima - DSC02187.JPG
image.alt: Grilled Hiroshima oysters served on Miyajima

foods.text: The region produces a significant share of Japan's oysters, grilled, fried or eaten raw, a defining local speciality.
foods.whereToTry: Miyajima's Omotesando street stalls, or dedicated oyster restaurants along Hiroshima's waterfront.

foods.name: Momiji manju
foods.text: Small maple-leaf-shaped cakes filled with sweet bean paste, custard or chocolate, a genuine Miyajima speciality sold throughout the island's old town.
foods.whereToTry: Omotesando street's bakeries, several offering fresh, warm versions made on the spot.

foods.name: Anagomeshi (conger eel rice)

image.alt: Anagomeshi, grilled conger eel served over rice

foods.text: Grilled conger eel served over rice, a genuine Miyajima and Hiroshima Bay speciality distinct from the more famous unagi freshwater eel.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional restaurants on Miyajima and along Hiroshima's waterfront, some over a century old.

foods.name: Hiroshima tsukemen

image.alt: A bowl of spicy dipping noodles, tsukemen-style

foods.text: A spicy dipping noodle dish distinct from Tokyo's own tsukemen style, with a local chilli oil base developed specifically in the city.
foods.whereToTry: Dedicated tsukemen restaurants throughout central Hiroshima.

foods.name: Saijo sake

image.alt: Hanahato, a sake brand from Saijo, Hiroshima

foods.text: A short train ride from Hiroshima, Saijo is one of Japan's most historically significant sake-brewing towns, its water prized by brewers for generations.
foods.whereToTry: Saijo's brewery district, several open for tastings and tours, or dedicated sake bars in central Hiroshima.

accommodation.intro: Basing in central Hiroshima keeps both the Peace Park and the Miyajima ferry within easy reach.

areas.name: Central Hiroshima, near the Peace Park
areas.text: The most central base, putting the Peace Park, museum and Dome within easy walking distance.

areas.name: Hiroshima Station area
areas.text: Excellent tram and rail connections, including the direct line out to Miyajimaguchi for the ferry.

areas.name: On Miyajima itself
areas.text: Staying overnight allows peaceful access to the shrine and old town after day-trippers depart on the evening ferry.

gettingThere.intro: Hiroshima sits directly on the shinkansen line, with Miyajima a short onward tram and ferry ride away.

options.text: Bullet trains connect Hiroshima to [[osaka-nara|Osaka]] in under 2 hours and to [[tokyo|Tokyo]] in about 4 hours.
options.detail: Hiroshima Station sits directly on the Sanyo Shinkansen line, making it an easy stop when travelling further into western Japan.

options.text: A limousine bus connects the airport to central Hiroshima in around 45 minutes, mainly serving domestic routes.
options.detail: Most international visitors arrive via shinkansen rather than flying directly into Hiroshima.

options.text: The Hiroden tram or JR train to Miyajimaguchi, then a short ferry crossing, takes about an hour door to door from central Hiroshima.
options.detail: Ferries run frequently throughout the day — no advance booking is generally needed outside peak holiday periods.

gettingAround.intro: Hiroshima's tram network covers the city well, and Miyajima's old town is compact and walkable.

options.text: A historic, still-functioning tram network connects the station, Peace Park and Miyajimaguchi ferry terminal directly.
options.detail: A day pass offers genuine value if making several tram journeys across the city.

options.text: The shrine, old town and ferry terminal all sit within a compact, walkable area.
options.detail: Mount Misen's cable car station requires a short bus or a longer uphill walk from the main village.

options.text: A two-stage cable car reaches close to Mount Misen's summit, with a final short walk required to the actual peak.
options.detail: Queues can build in peak season — an early start helps avoid the longest waits.

bestTime.headline: March–May and October–November, for mild weather and clear island views
bestTime.summary: Hiroshima and Miyajima share a comfortable climate in spring and autumn, with clearer skies benefiting both the memorial sites and Mount Misen's views.

seasons.text: Cherry blossoms around the Peace Park and comfortable temperatures, with manageable crowds outside Golden Week.
Hot and humid, though the 6 August Peace Memorial Ceremony draws genuine international attention if the date aligns with your trip.
Comfortable temperatures and spectacular foliage on Miyajima's Momijidani Park, arguably the island's most beautiful season.
Cold but usually clear, with peaceful, uncrowded access to both the Peace Park and Miyajima's shrine.

bestTime.avoid: Golden Week and peak summer weekends without ferry and accommodation timing checked ahead, when Miyajima's crossing and old town both get crowded.

itinerary.title: Two days in Hiroshima and Miyajima
itinerary.intro: The Peace Park and its history first, then Miyajima's shrine and mountain.

days.title: Hiroshima's Peace Memorial sites
days.summary: A direct, honest look at the city's history.
days.afternoon: The Peace Memorial Park and the Atomic Bomb Dome.

days.title: Miyajima island
days.summary: The floating torii gate and Mount Misen.
days.morning: Ferry to Miyajima and Itsukushima Shrine.
days.afternoon: Mount Misen by cable car and a short summit hike.
days.evening: Grilled oysters and momiji manju on Omotesando before the last ferry back.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on timing, tides and etiquette that make a real difference to a Hiroshima and Miyajima trip.
tips: Check Miyajima's tide tables before your visit — high tide floats the torii gate, low tide lets you walk out to it.
Allow at least two hours for the Peace Memorial Museum — its content deserves unhurried time.
Don't feed Miyajima's deer, unlike Nara's — it's actively discouraged on the island.
Take the last ferry back from Miyajima seriously — services thin out in the evening, especially outside peak season.
Visit Okonomimura for an easy way to compare several Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki stalls in one stop.
Book Golden Week and summer weekend accommodation on Miyajima well ahead, when the island's limited rooms sell out.
Consider a day trip to Saijo for sake tasting if staying three or more nights in the area.

faq.q: How many days do you need for Hiroshima and Miyajima?
faq.a: Two works well — one full day for the Peace Memorial sites, one for Miyajima's shrine and Mount Misen.

faq.q: Is the Peace Memorial Museum difficult to visit?
faq.a: It's sobering and substantial, but presented with real honesty and educational care — most visitors find it a valuable, moving part of understanding the city and the period.

faq.q: Is Miyajima worth visiting as a day trip from Hiroshima?
faq.a: Yes, it works well as a day trip given the roughly hour-long journey, though an overnight stay allows quieter access to the shrine and old town after other visitors depart.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: March to May and October to November offer the best weather — cherry blossoms in spring, comfortable temperatures and spectacular foliage on Miyajima in autumn.

faq.q: Is Hiroshima worth visiting beyond the Peace Memorial sites?
faq.a: Yes — the city's food culture, particularly its own okonomiyaki style, and its resilient, forward-looking modern character are worthwhile independent of the memorial sites.
